title: The Guardian Reported Missing FBI Memos in Epstein-File Release
description_medium: On February 26, 2026, The Guardian reported that it had obtained three FBI Form 302 memoranda describing four 2019 interviews, records absent from the Justice Department’s Epstein-file release. The interviews included an explicit but unsubstantiated allegation about Trump. The Guardian said the FBI brought no charges related to it, the allegation had not been verified, and Trump denied wrongdoing.
description_long:
The Guardian reported on February 26, 2026, that it had obtained three FBI Form 302 memoranda memorializing 25 pages of agents’ notes from four interviews conducted in 2019. The Justice Department had not included those records when it uploaded millions of Epstein-related files. The Guardian described the records as containing an explicit allegation against Donald Trump, but emphasized that it was unsubstantiated and unverified; the FBI brought no charges related to the claim, and Trump has denied wrongdoing.

The report said only the first interview was in the public release, and that interview did not name Trump. An administration official confirmed the missing reports were authentic and told the Guardian the department considered the files duplicative and not legally required to be released. The DOJ also told NPR that nothing had been deleted and withheld records were duplicative or privileged. Congressional Democrats sought an accounting, and the Republican oversight chair said lawmakers would examine the matter. The reporting documents a dispute about specific records and the department’s release process; it does not establish why the records were omitted or validate the allegation.
evidence_notes: Read The Guardian report. It says three authentic Form 302s recorded four 2019 interviews, were not included in DOJ's release, and contained an unverified allegation; no charge arose and Trump denied wrongdoing. DOJ/admin official described them as duplicative/privileged. Allegation not reported as fact.
corrected_wording: Retitled around the specific missing FBI records; removed unrelated claims about Trump prioritizing momentum or directing disclosure.

title: House Oversight Members Sought an Accounting of Missing Epstein FBI Memos
description_medium: The Guardian reported that three FBI interview memoranda about Epstein were absent from the Justice Department’s public release. After earlier reporting drew attention to the files, House Oversight Democrats said they would investigate and Rep. Robert Garcia asked Attorney General Pam Bondi for a full accounting. The missing records contained an unverified allegation, not a finding of fact.
description_long:
The Guardian’s February 26, 2026 report on missing Epstein-related FBI interview memoranda also described a congressional response. Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said he had reviewed unredacted evidence logs at the Justice Department but could not locate the records. He wrote Attorney General Pam Bondi demanding a full accounting of why the documents had not been released. The Guardian reported that House Oversight Democrats would open an investigation into DOJ’s handling; committee chair James Comer, a Republican, also said lawmakers would look into the issue.

The records at issue were three FBI Form 302 reports documenting four interviews from 2019. They included an explicit allegation against Donald Trump, which The Guardian characterized as unsubstantiated and said had not been verified; the FBI filed no charges related to it, and Trump has denied wrongdoing. An administration official described the documents as duplicative and said they were not legally required to be released. The reporting therefore documents a dispute over the public file and a request for oversight, not proof of a cover-up, the underlying allegation, or the department’s motive.
evidence_notes: The Guardian reports Rep. Robert Garcia's letter to AG Pam Bondi and planned House Oversight Democratic investigation; Comer also said lawmakers would look into the issue. The article's underlying unsubstantiated allegation is clearly qualified. Same report as entry-1786, but this description focuses on the oversight response.
corrected_wording: Retitled around the documented congressional response and replaced unsupported narrative-control/institutional-clarity claims.

title: PolitiFact Rated About 19% of Its Tracked Trump Promises as Kept
description_medium: A February 2026 PolitiFact analysis tested Trump’s claim that he had kept all his campaign promises against a tracker of 75 second-term pledges. It rated about 19% as kept, while many remained in progress or stalled; one broken promise was to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours. PolitiFact said its status ratings assess outcomes, not whether a promise was desirable.
description_long:
In February 2026, President Donald Trump said he had kept all of his campaign promises. PolitiFact’s MAGA-Meter compared that claim with a tracker of 75 promises from his second-term campaign. The tracker sorted pledges into five categories: Stalled, In the Works, Promise Kept, Promise Broken, and Compromise. At the time of the analysis, about 19% were rated kept; roughly 45% were still in progress and about 31% were stalled. PolitiFact also listed the promise to end the Russia-Ukraine war within 24 hours as broken after the war continued and U.S.-brokered talks in Geneva did not produce a resolution.

The comparison offers a defined set and explicit status labels for evaluating Trump’s absolute claim. PolitiFact said the ratings were not a value judgment about whether the promises themselves should have been kept. The percentages are a snapshot of the 75 pledges tracked in that report, not a measure of every campaign statement or overall presidential performance. The evidence supports contrasting Trump’s claim with the tracker’s recorded outcomes; it does not support the former entry’s assertion that criteria were ambiguous or that promise coverage prioritized momentum over deliberation.
evidence_notes: PolitiFact report summarized by PBS and available directly: 75 second-term pledges, five explicit status labels, about 19% kept; analysis also notes broken 24-hour Ukraine-war promise. Statuses are outcomes, not value judgments.
corrected_wording: Retitled around the specific tracker result and replaced false claims of ambiguous criteria/high-voltage messaging with the tracker’s published scope and status categories.

title: Project 2025 Proposed Expanded Federal Reporting on Abortions
description_medium: Project 2025 called for a federal mandate requiring states to collect extensive information on every abortion provided. This is a policy recommendation, not an implemented CDC reporting system. CDC says state submission of abortion data is voluntary, while most states separately collect provider reports under state law. The proposal would expand federal reporting; the supplied sources do not show that it became a nationwide requirement.
description_long:
Project 2025’s reproductive-health agenda proposed requiring every state to collect extensive information on abortions and submit it under a federal mandate. The Guttmacher Institute described the plan as a proposed expansion of abortion reporting and raised privacy concerns about the information states might collect. The distinction is important: existing CDC abortion surveillance depends on voluntary state submissions, and reporting requirements vary under state laws. CDC states that there is no national requirement for jurisdictions to submit abortion data.

The sources support describing an expansion proposal and the existing patchwork of reporting. They do not show that the Trump administration created a federal database, mandated the specific fields listed in the original long description, or required states to track miscarriages, contraception, or all pregnancy outcomes. Nor do they document an enacted system used to prosecute patients or providers. The proposal remains distinct from current state-level reporting and the CDC’s voluntary surveillance program; the Guttmacher analysis frames the proposed expansion as a privacy concern.
evidence_notes: Guttmacher says Project 2025 calls for a federal mandate on extensive information for every abortion; CDC FAQ says there is no national requirement for state data submission. The sources support a proposal and current voluntary/variable reporting, not an implemented Trump surveillance system.
corrected_wording: Retitled and rewrote as a Project 2025 proposal; removed unsupported claims that CDC had implemented a federal personal-health database or expanded reporting to miscarriages, contraception, and other outcomes.

title: Lawmakers Move to Ban DHS WRAP Restraints After Trump-Era Detention Abuses
description_medium: Rep. Delia Ramirez introduced the Full-Body Restraint Prohibition Act on February 25, 2026. It would bar DHS from buying or using the WRAP restraint and add oversight and reporting requirements. The proposal followed AP reporting that ICE used the device on deportation flights and lacked use data. Introduction of the bill does not mean the ban became law.
description_long:
On February 25, 2026, Rep. Delia Ramirez introduced the Full-Body Restraint Prohibition Act, which would bar the Department of Homeland Security from buying or using the WRAP full-body restraint and add oversight and reporting requirements. The proposal followed an Associated Press investigation into the device. AP reported that ICE had used WRAP restraints on deportation flights since 2020, sometimes for hours, and that a dozen local-law-enforcement deaths over the prior decade involved autopsies linking the device to the outcome. A 2023 DHS civil-rights report had raised internal concerns about the restraint.

DHS was not tracking ICE’s use as required for force reporting, so AP could not determine how many people had been restrained during deportation flights. The bill sought to address the use and oversight gap; advocates and the device’s maker offered competing views about safety. This entry records the bill at introduction and the reporting that prompted it. The source does not establish that Congress passed it, that DHS changed its rules, or that the proposal had taken effect.
evidence_notes: AP report summary states bill introduction on Feb. 25, ICE flight use since 2020, local autopsy-linked deaths, and a 2023 DHS civil-rights concern; no later legislative status in linked story. Text accurately marks it as a proposal.
corrected_wording: Replaced generalized centralization/long-tail claims with the bill’s provisions, AP’s documented use/oversight facts, and its introduced-only status.
